description_full: The Walt Disney Company operates as an entertainment company in Americas, Europe, and the Asia Pacific. It operates in three segments: Entertainment, Sports, and Experiences. The company produces and distributes film and television content under the ABC Television Network, Disney, Freeform, FX, Fox, National Geographic, and Star brand television channels, as well as ABC television stations and A+E television networks; and produces original content under the Disney Branded Television, FX Productions, Lucasfilm, Marvel, National Geographic Studios, Pixar, Searchlight Pictures, Twentieth Century Studios, 20th Television, and Walt Disney Pictures banners. It also provides direct-to-consumer streaming services through Disney+, Disney+ Hotstar, and Hulu; sports-related video streaming content through ESPN, ESPN on ABC, ESPN+ DTC, and Star; sale/licensing of film and episodic content to television and video-on-demand services; theatrical, home entertainment, and music distribution services; DVD and Blu-ray discs, electronic home video licenses, and VOD rental services; staging and licensing of live entertainment events; and post-production services. In addition, the company operates theme parks and resorts, such as Walt Disney World Resort, Disneyland Resort, Disneyland Paris, Hong Kong Disneyland Resort, Shanghai Disney Resort, Disney Cruise Line, Disney Vacation Club, National Geographic Expeditions, and Adventures by Disney, as well as Aulani, a Disney resort and spa in Hawaii. Further, it licenses its intellectual property (IP) to a third party that owns and operates Tokyo Disney Resort; licenses trade names, characters, visual, literary, and other IP for use on merchandise, published materials, and games; operates a direct-to-home satellite distribution platform; sells branded merchandise through retail, online, and wholesale businesses; and develops and publishes books, comic books, and magazines. The company was founded in 1923 and is based in Burbank, California.

financial_summary: Walt Disney Company (The) is a mega-cap communication services business with a $201.6B market cap on $94.4B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests.

The business throws off $10.1B in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.46× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.6× net debt/EBITDA.

Shareholder yield of 2.6% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 10pp above the Communication Services median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It earns less of the sector's profit than its revenue share would suggest (0.91x).
It accounts for 3.9% of sector revenue and 3.5% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.06 across 169 companies in the universe; the top four hold 36% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 27% and a beta of 1.05, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $799.2M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 42% in the 2020 crash, 47% in the 2022 bear market and 55% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $51.11 (margin of safety -128%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 23%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $32.12 to $79.32 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Communication Services peers: P/E 24.1 vs 14.9, EV/EBITDA 11.9 vs 9.4 and P/FCF 20.0 vs 11.3 (sector median).
The EBIT multiple is close to its own 10-year median (-5%).
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 5.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 7.0% (vs the 8% bar).
The 32 covering analysts target $127 on average, 8% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 7% falls short of the cost of capital of 9.3%, so growth at these returns destroys value; returns have been steady (CV 0.28).
It converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.46x.
ROE of 11% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.8x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 1.6x net debt to EBITDA ($5.7B of cash against $42.0B of debt), above the 1.5x gate.
The current ratio of 0.71 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 37% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.5% over 3 years and 7.6% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 12% of profits supports about 0.9% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 22.9% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00 and a backlog worth 17% of annual revenue.
Capex runs 1.5x depreciation (8.5% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 79%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $5.8M sold).
It returns 2.6% a year to shareholders (1.7% in buybacks and 1.3% in dividends).
people: With about 175,560 employees, each generates about $538K of revenue, in line with the Communication Services median, and productivity has risen 5.2% a year.
That works out to $57K of free cash flow per employee.
